outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the icosahedral and dodecahedral parts have changed: Pollock's stated constants 13 and 21 are shown false by counterexamples (95 and 79), and corrected sharp bounds 15 and 22 are claimed proved (IMRN 2025, re-posted to arXiv 8 Aug 2026), with a computational gap I could not close. The tetrahedral part remains open with no proof found, the octahedral part remains open below e^(10⁷), the cube part (1909–1912) and centered nonagonal part (2023, generalised 2025) were settled before this window, and no AI system is named for any in-window result.
problem_asks: Parts of the Pollock conjectures as listed in the current Wikipedia article (the frozen bullet names only 'Pollock's conjectures'). (a) Tetrahedral: every positive integer is a sum of at most 5 tetrahedral numbers, n(n+1)(n+2)/6. (b) Tetrahedral, second part as the sources state it: all but finitely many integers are sums of at most 4 tetrahedral numbers, equivalently the exception list (OEIS A000797) is finite; conjectured 241 terms, largest 343867. (c) Octahedral: every positive integer is a sum of at most 7 octahedral numbers, n(2n²+1)/3. (d) Cubes: every positive integer is a sum of at most 9 positive cubes. (e) Icosahedral: every positive integer is a sum of at most 13 icosahedral numbers, n(5n²−5n+2)/2. (f) Dodecahedral: every positive integer is a sum of at most 21 dodecahedral numbers. (g) Centered nonagonal: every positive integer is a sum of at most 11 centered nonagonal numbers. Parts (a)–(f) are Pollock's Platonic-solid claims; (g) is in the same article. I did not check whether the January 2024 revision listed (e)–(g) (Wayback is blocked), so that is unverified.

events.what_happened: Zarathustra Brady, 'Sums of seven octahedral numbers' (single author). Shows every integer greater than e^(10⁷) is a sum of seven positive octahedral numbers, as a special case of a broad class of cubic polynomials f, and says this reduces Pollock's octahedral claim to a finite computation below that bound. Appeared on arXiv as 1509.04316 and in J. London Math. Soc. 93(1), 2016, pp. 244–272 (DOI 10.1112/jlms/jdv061). The arXiv listing has an ancillary C++ file (walk.cpp), which I did not open.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 14 Sep 2015; v2 16 Sep 2015 ('Ancillary file added'); journal version JLMS 93(1), 1 Feb 2016.
events.delivers: Octahedral part for all integers n greater than e^(10⁷) only. Does not touch the positive integers at or below e^(10⁷).
events.remains: Every positive integer up to e^(10⁷), so 'every positive integer is a sum of at most 7 octahedral numbers' is not established by this event. Basak et al. (arXiv 2608.08019, Section 1, as quoted in a search summary) say the threshold is beyond current computation.

checked_by.who: Journal of the London Mathematical Society
checked_by.where: https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.04316 (journal reference on the arXiv abstract page; the JLMS page itself was not opened)

events.direction: Supports the octahedral claim for sufficiently large n. No counterexample and no claim against the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Herbert E. Salzer and Norman Levine, a table of integers up to 10⁶ that are not sums of four tetrahedral numbers, Math. Comp. 12 (1958) 141–144. OEIS and MathWorld attribute to them the conjecture that exactly 241 integers need five tetrahedral numbers, the largest being 343867. Not opened; taken from OEIS A000797 and MathWorld.
events.delivers: A finite table (to 10⁶) of exceptions to the four-term representation, and the conjectural claim that the exception list has exactly 241 terms with maximum 343867.
events.remains: The five-term claim for all integers; the finiteness of the exception list beyond the table range.
events.directly_checkable: The 241 exceptions are listed in OEIS A000797 ('The 241 known terms', McCranie and Wilson), which can be checked by computer.
events.direction: Supports the four-term exception list up to 10⁶. Does not contradict the five-term claim.

events.what_happened: Chung Chiang Chou and Yuefan Deng, 'Decomposing 40 billion integers by four tetrahedral numbers', Math. Comp. 66(218), April 1997, pp. 893–901. A computer search on a massively parallel supercomputer finds that every integer n with 343,867 < n < 40 billion is a sum of at most four tetrahedral numbers. The abstract says this improves an earlier bound of 10⁹ obtained a year before. The Stony Brook record reproduces the abstract (opened); the paper itself was not opened.
events.delivers: Finite-range verification of the four-term claim: every integer in (343867, 4×10¹⁰) is a sum of at most four tetrahedral numbers. Does not decide the five-term claim for all integers, nor the four-term claim above 4×10¹⁰.
events.remains: The five-term claim for all integers; the four-term claim for n ≥ 4×10¹⁰ (the Chou–Deng belief, cited in arXiv 0806.2486, that every n > 343867 is a sum of four tetrahedral numbers).
events.directly_checkable: The computation is a search over integers, not an object exhibited by hand.
events.direction: Supports the four-term claim over a finite range. No counterexample to the five-term claim.

events.what_happened: Arthur Wieferich, a proof that every integer is a sum of at most nine positive cubes, Math. Ann. 66 (1909) 95–101. Wikipedia's Pollock article credits this as the cube case. Not opened; taken from Wikipedia and a Waring's-problem search summary.
events.delivers: Every positive integer is a sum of at most nine positive cubes (g(3)=9), subject to the gap noted in doubts.
events.remains: Nothing of part (d), if the completion by Kempner (1912) is accepted.

checked_by.who: Mathematische Annalen (journal of record); later completed by Kempner (1912) and, per the Vavilov survey, Dickson (1927)
checked_by.qualification: Peer-reviewed journal; Kempner and Dickson are named specialists in Waring's problem
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the proof; Kempner filled a gap; Dickson filled a further gap (per the survey cited in search)

events.doubts: Sources disagree on whether Wieferich's proof was complete as published: the Vavilov survey says gaps were filled by Kempner (1912) and Dickson (1927). A lean-lang.org eval page titled 'Wieferich's theorem g(3) = 9' appeared in search; I did not open it, so no machine check is claimed.
events.object: Lower bound: 23 needs nine positive cubes (standard example, from a search summary). The upper bound is a general proof.

events.what_happened: Aubrey John Kempner, Math. Ann. 72 (1912) 387–399, completing the proof that every integer is a sum of at most nine positive cubes. Sources give different titles ('Bemerkungen zum Waringschen Problem' on ProofWiki; 'Über das Waringsche Problem und einige Verallgemeinerungen' on a Lean page) and different dates (Britannica 1912; ProofWiki 1909–1921). Not opened.
events.delivers: Fills the remaining gap in Wieferich's argument, giving the nine-cube result (per Wikipedia and the Vavilov survey).
events.doubts: The gap-filling claim rests on secondary descriptions; I did not open the 1912 paper.

events.what_happened: Maya Mohsin Ahmed, 'A Platonic basis of Integers', arXiv 1904.02787 (3 Apr 2019, one version). Proves that every integer is an integer combination of exactly four tetrahedral numbers. The abstract was opened; the body was not read.
events.delivers: Every integer as a signed combination of four tetrahedral numbers. A different question: Pollock asks for sums of at most five non-negative tetrahedral numbers.
events.remains: The non-negative five-term claim for all positive integers, and the finiteness of the exception list.
events.direction: Different question (signed combinations); neither supports nor contradicts the non-negative claim.

events.what_happened: Vadim Ponomarenko, 'Pollock's Generalized Tetrahedral Numbers Conjecture', Amer. Math. Monthly 128(10), December 2021, p. 921 (citation from a search summary). With tetrahedral numbers indexed by all integers, every integer is a sum of at most four such numbers, via an identity using indices n, n−2, −n−1 (twice). A 2021 draft PDF on vadim.sdsu.edu was seen only as a search snippet and not opened.
events.revisions: A 2021 draft PDF exists; the earliest date for the argument was not established.
events.delivers: Four generalized tetrahedral numbers (indices in all of Z) always suffice. A changed question: negative indices are allowed. Does not address the positive-integer claim.
events.remains: The positive-index five-term claim and the finiteness part.

checked_by.where: https://vadim.sdsu.edu/maa-pollock-v3.pdf (draft seen in search; not opened)

events.direction: Different question; no counterexample to Pollock's positive-index claim.

events.what_happened: R. Lycan and V. Ponomarenko, 'Sums of Two Generalized Tetrahedral Numbers', PUMP Journal of Undergraduate Research (2022): a method to compute sums of two generalized tetrahedral numbers up to a bound, and which perfect powers are such sums. A separate Ponomarenko note, undated in my sources, shows two generalized tetrahedral numbers do not suffice in general and asks whether three do. Neither was opened.
events.delivers: Computations and partial results for the two-term generalized (all-integer index) problem. A different question.
events.direction: Different question; no bearing on the positive-integer claim.

events.what_happened: Miroslav Kureš, 'A Proof of Pollock's Conjecture on Centered Nonagonal Numbers', The Mathematical Intelligencer, DOI 10.1007/s00283-023-10307-0. Every natural number is a sum of at most 11 centered nonagonal numbers. A Brno University of Technology record gives a release date of 27 Oct 2023; Wikipedia cites vol. 46 issue 3 (2024). The Springer page redirected and was not opened; details come from search snippets and Wikipedia.
events.delivers: Pollock's centered nonagonal claim as stated (n=9, at most 11 summands, all natural numbers). Settles that part of the bullet.

checked_by.qualification: Journal of record for short research notes

events.direction: Confirms Pollock's claim as stated for n=9.

events.what_happened: arXiv 2412.13974, 'On the order of 4-dimensional regular polytope numbers' (posted Dec 2024, per the arXiv listing in a search result). Bounds the order of regular polytope numbers of the six convex regular 4-polytopes (Corollary 1.3: G({3,4,3}), G({3,3,5}), G({5,3,3}) ≤ 17), and gives a degree-four polynomial result via the circle method. Abstract-level snippet only; the Pollock conjectures are not mentioned in what I saw.
events.delivers: Order bounds for regular polytope numbers of 4-polytopes. Not Pollock's polyhedral (3-dimensional Platonic) numbers. Discarded as a different question.

events.what_happened: Anji Dong, Katerina Saettone, Kendra Song, Alexandru Zaharescu, 'Cannonball Polygons with Multiplicities', arXiv 2507.18057, posted 24 Jul 2025 (per a search summary). Generalises the cannonball problem with weight functions; Theorem 1.1 gives cannonball polygons of multiplicity 8 with a prescribed largest side. Abstract-level only; keywords include square-pyramidal numbers.
events.delivers: Cannonball-type results with multiplicities (sums of squares structure). A different problem; not one of Pollock's polyhedral statements.

events.what_happened: Reported only: a 2024 preprint by Basak, Dong, Saettone and Zaharescu titled 'Pollock's Conjectures on Icosahedral and Dodecahedral Numbers'. This comes from search summaries, one of which says the GitHub README cites it as 'Preprint, 2024' with a Google Drive link. I opened that README: it cites only the IMRN 2025 paper and no preprint. Not located.
events.doubts: Existence unverified. The OUP page says the IMRN paper was received 26 Sep 2024, so an earlier draft is plausible; if a public 2024 version exists, the first-argument date of the IMRN work would be earlier than the date I use, and it may fall on either side of 26 Jan 2024.

events.what_happened: M. V. Nedoshev and V. V. Kyrychenko, 'Peculiarities of the Operation of Complex Computational Algorithms using the Example of Testing the Polock Hypothesis' (Ukrainian title: 'Особливості роботи складних обчислювальних алгоритмів на прикладі перевірки гіпотези Полокка'), Central Ukrainian Scientific Bulletin (Technical Sciences) 11(42) part II (2025), pp. 23–29, DOI 10.32515/2664-262X.2025.11(42).2.23-29. From the front matter in search: algorithms for writing integers as sums of tetrahedral numbers, with greedy, two-pointer, memoisation and multithreading methods and a performance comparison. The full PDF and journal page were not opened.
events.delivers: Algorithms and timing for testing whether integers are sums of tetrahedral numbers. The front matter I saw states no new mathematical resolution, and I do not know its tested range.
events.doubts: Not read beyond front matter; whether it claims a verification range is unknown.
events.direction: Computational testing of the tetrahedral hypothesis; does not decide it on the front matter seen.

events.what_happened: Benjamin Lee Warren and Miroslav Kureš, 'Every positive integer is a sum of at most n+2 centered n-gonal numbers', Mathematica Slovaca 75(3) (2025) 515–524, DOI 10.1515/ms-2025-0037. A corrigendum appeared Aug 2025 (search summary). For n=9 the bound is 11, so Pollock's nonagonal claim is a special case. The De Gruyter PDF returned an error and was not opened; content is from search summaries and Wikipedia.
events.delivers: Every positive integer is a sum of at most n+2 centered n-gonal numbers, for all n. The n=9 case is Pollock's claim, already settled in 2023.
events.remains: Nothing of part (g) beyond the 2023 result.
events.direction: Confirms Pollock's nonagonal claim as a special case of a general theorem.

events.what_happened: Debmalya Basak, Anji Dong, Katerina Saettone, Alexandru Zaharescu, 'Representations as Sums of Icosahedral and Dodecahedral Numbers: Proof of Pollock's Conjectures', IMRN 2025(13), article rnaf180, DOI 10.1093/imrn/rnaf180. The OUP page (opened) gives received 26 Sep 2024, revised 28 May 2025, accepted 3 Jun 2025, published 27 Jun 2025. The full text is paywalled. I read the arXiv copy 2608.08019, which has the same title, authors, abstract and journal reference. Its Section 1 states Pollock's 1843 claims (≤13 icosahedral, ≤21 dodecahedral) and proves refined versions: Theorem 1.7 (every positive integer is a sum of at most 15 icosahedral numbers, and 15 is minimal), Theorem 1.8 (at most 22 dodecahedral, 22 minimal), Theorems 1.1–1.2 (asymptotic counts for nine summands, m > e^(e^94)), and Theorems 1.5–1.6 (eight summands for m ≥ 10³⁶ icosahedral and m ≥ 10³⁹ dodecahedral). Verification up to a stated bound is referred to in Section 1 and in the GitHub README.
events.revisions: Earliest public version I could verify is the IMRN online publication (27 Jun 2025). A 2024 preprint is reported but not located (see preprint-2024-reported-unverified). arXiv copy posted 8 Aug 2026 (see arxiv-2026-08-08-repost).
events.delivers: Claims that Pollock's constants are too small and that the sharp constants are 15 for icosahedral and 22 for dodecahedral numbers, with minimality. The 15 and 22 claims for all integers rest partly on computation, which the GitHub README gives as below 9.6446×10³⁵ (icosahedral) and below 5.04×10³⁸ (dodecahedral). The analytic eight-summand results start at 10³⁶ and 10³⁹. Restrictions: the bounds are corrected constants, not 13 and 21.
events.remains: Pollock's stated 13 and 21 are not established by this paper (they are refuted, see object). Its 15 and 22 claims for all integers are, per the README, computational below 9.6446×10³⁵ and 5.04×10³⁸, so the windows [9.6446×10³⁵, 10³⁶) for icosahedral and [5.04×10³⁸, 10³⁹) for dodecahedral are not covered by the text I read, unless a section I could not read covers them. The tetrahedral and octahedral parts (a)–(c) are outside this paper.

checked_by.who: International Mathematics Research Notices (Oxford University Press)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper on 3 Jun 2025 after refereeing; referee identities are not in the sources I could read

checked_by.who: Pith automated AI referee (the site names the model as deepseek-v4-flash)
checked_by.qualification: None. It is an AI model, not a human reader
checked_by.what_they_did: Read the arXiv copy on 12 Aug 2026. Verdict: the eight-term Linnik analysis is a real advance, but the sharp 15/22 claims rest on an unpublished computation and the nine-term asymptotics have an error term that swamps the main term. States: 'No human expert has reviewed this paper yet.'

events.time_since_posted: About 15 months since IMRN publication; about 2 months since the arXiv posting
events.directly_checkable: Witnesses for the sharpness claims: 95 = 48 + 3·12 + 11·1 uses 15 icosahedral numbers (1, 12, 48 are the only icosahedral numbers ≤ 95), and no representation with fewer exists, so 95 refutes 13. 79 = 3·20 + 19·1 uses 22 dodecahedral numbers (1 and 20 are the only dodecahedral numbers ≤ 79), and none fewer exists, so 79 refutes 21. I checked these by hand from the formulas in the search results; the refined bounds for all integers are not hand-checkable.
events.doubts: (1) The AI referee says the sharp 15/22 claims rest on an unpublished computation: Section 9.3 cites an author's webpage [7] with no code or data. I could not read Section 9.3 myself. (2) The GitHub README gives computed ranges 9.6446×10³⁵ and 5.04×10³⁸, below the thresholds 10³⁶ and 10³⁹ in Theorems 1.5 and 1.6. Unless another argument covers the gap, the 15 and 22 claims for those windows are not supported by the text I read. This is my reading of two secondary figures, not a verified gap. (3) The AI referee says the asymptotic error terms in Theorems 1.1–1.2 exceed the main term in the stated range; I could not check this. (4) The date conflict: IMRN 2025 versus arXiv 8 Aug 2026; the author's homepage lists the paper as 'accepted for publication (2025)' while linking the arXiv number.
events.direction: Against Pollock's stated constants 13 and 21: the 2026 preprints name 95 and 79 as counterexamples. For the corrected constants 15 and 22: the paper claims they are proved and minimal.
events.object: No single object. The minimality of the corrected bounds is witnessed by 95 (needs 15 icosahedral numbers) and 79 (needs 22 dodecahedral numbers), which the admissible-pairs preprint cites as counterexamples to Pollock's 13 and 21. The discoverer and date of these witnesses are not in any source I read. Whether the IMRN text states them I could not check. The proof itself is analytic plus computational.

ai.note: No source I read names an AI system as a contributor. The only AI involvement found is the automated Pith AI referee review (12 Aug 2026), which is checking and not part of the mathematics, so it is not listed in systems. The full text, including any acknowledgements, could not be read.

events.what_happened: Anji Dong, Vi Anh Nguyen, Alexandru Zaharescu, 'Admissible Pairs: A Variation to Pollock Conjectures', arXiv 2608.03309 (submitted 4 Aug 2026, one version, math.NT). For two polyhedral forms f and h, a pair (u, v) is admissible if every positive integer is a sum of at most u values of f and at most v values of h. For icosahedral and dodecahedral numbers, Theorem 1.5 says the essential pairs are exactly the twelve pairs of Conjecture 1.3: (5,6), (4,7), (3,8), (2,9), (1,11), (0,22), (6,5), (7,4), (8,3), (9,2), (10,1), (15,0). The introduction says Pollock's icosahedral conjecture is false, with counterexample 95 requiring 15 terms, and cites Basak et al. [2] for corrected constants g(I)=15 and g(D)=22. Computation: Algorithm I checks the first 12000 integers and Algorithm II completes the remaining pairs (GitHub README). The fetched text rendered the counterexample numbers with doubled digits (9595 and 7979); I read them as 95 and 79 from the search summaries and from my hand check.
events.delivers: A variation (two-form mixed sums): for (icosahedral, dodecahedral) it identifies the complete list of essential pairs. Its special cases (15,0) and (0,22) are the corrected pure statements of part (e) and part (f). It does not restate Pollock's 13 or 21.
events.remains: Parts (a)–(d) and the finiteness part (b) are untouched. The pure statements (13, 21) are not reinstated.
events.directly_checkable: Computational: a Python script (Algorithm I.py) checks the first 12000 integers; Algorithm II folder contains four scripts. The repository has 20 commits and no visible dates.
events.doubts: Relies on computation whose full range and correctness readers must trust: Algorithm I is slow beyond about 10⁵, and Algorithm II is used for the rest. The README says (15,0) and (0,22) are 'already checked in one of the references', so the variation is not independent of the corrected-bound work in the IMRN paper.
events.direction: Variation with no counterexample. Consistent with the corrected pure bounds 15 and 22 and with the refutation of 13 and 21.
events.object: No single object. The explicit essential-pair list is the result. Corrected pure witnesses are 95 (15 icosahedral) and 79 (22 dodecahedral) as above.

events.doubts: Same doubts as imrn-2025-basak-icosahedral-dodecahedral. The arXiv date (2026) and the journal reference (2025) do not match, and I could not resolve why.

disputes.summary: Pollock's statements are dated 1843 by Brady (2015), by the arXiv 2608.08019 abstract, and in MathWorld's 1843–1850 reference; they are dated 1850 by Wikipedia, OEIS A000797 and MathWorld's tetrahedral text. OEIS cites Pollock's paper as Proc. Roy. Soc. London 5 (1851) 922–924. I record both and pick neither.

Wikipedia says the icosahedral and dodecahedral conjectures were 'corrected and confirmed true in 2025', citing the IMRN 2025 paper. The arXiv copy is dated 8 Aug 2026 and carries the IMRN 2025 journal reference. The author's homepage lists the paper as 'accepted for publication (2025)'. Which date is the first public version is unresolved, so the events carry both dates.

Cube case: Wikipedia credits Wieferich (1909) and Kempner (1912). Britannica (via search) dates the result to 1912 with Wieferich and Kempner. ProofWiki gives 1909–1921. The Vavilov survey says Kempner (1912) and Dickson (1927) filled gaps in Wieferich's proof.
A 2024 preprint with the icosahedral/dodecahedral title is reported in search summaries; the GitHub README I opened cites only the IMRN 2025 paper.

The fetched text of arXiv 2608.03309 shows the counterexamples with doubled digits (9595, 1515 terms; 7979, 2222 terms) and '1200012000' for the 12000 check. The README and search summaries give 95 (15 terms), 79 (22 terms) and 12000. I use 95, 79 and 12000 and confirmed the minimal counts by hand.

summary: Forty-three queries were run across arXiv (2608.08019, 2608.03309, 1509.04316, 1904.02787, and listings), the IMRN/OUP page, Wikipedia (the Pollock article, which I fetched in its current form, and the icosahedral-number article), OEIS A282350 and A000797, MathWorld, the Stony Brook record of the 1997 Chou–Deng paper, John D. Cook's blog, the Pith review, the authors' homepage, two GitHub repositories, and an AI-results tracker. Blocked or unreadable sources: zbMATH, Springer, ACM, De Gruyter, Wayback, the arXiv author page, the arXiv PDFs of 2608.08019/2608.03309/2608.29595, and the AlphaEvolve PDF (too large). Since 26 Jan 2024 the icosahedral and dodecahedral parts have changed. Pollock's stated constants 13 and 21 are shown false: the 2026 preprints name 95 (15 icosahedral numbers needed) and 79 (22 dodecahedral needed), and I confirmed both minimal counts by hand. The corrected bounds 15 and 22 are claimed proved, with minimality, in an IMRN 2025 paper (received 26 Sep 2024, accepted 3 Jun 2025, published 27 Jun 2025), re-posted to arXiv on 8 Aug 2026. Wikipedia records this as 'corrected and confirmed true in 2025'. The paper's own computational ranges, as given in the GitHub README (below 9.6446×10³⁵ and 5.04×10³⁸), fall short of the 10³⁶ and 10³⁹ thresholds of its eight-summand theorems, so a window in each case seems to need separate coverage. I could not read Section 9.3 to check. An AI referee on Pith (12 Aug 2026) raises this, and the unpublished-computation and error-term points, and states no human had reviewed the paper; I record it as automated and do not treat it as a verdict. The admissible-pairs variation (arXiv 2608.03309, 4 Aug 2026) determines the essential pairs for the icosahedral and dodecahedral case, including (15,0) and (0,22), as special cases. The tetrahedral part is open: I found no proof, the 2025 Nedoshev–Kyrychenko paper is algorithmic, and a 2024 verification to 4.71×10²⁰ that appeared in a search summary could not be located. The octahedral part is proven only for n above e^(10⁷) (Brady 2015/2016), and I found no progress on the finite range. The cube part (1909–1912) and the centered-nonagonal part (Kureš 2023; Warren–Kureš 2025 generalisation) were settled before this window. On AI: no source I read names an AI system for any Pollock result. The only AI-related item is the Pith referee, which I treat as checking, not as contribution; the full text of the 2026 preprints, including acknowledgements, could not be read, so this is the main gap. Close calls: (i) whether 'the problem' is the 1843 wording, which is refuted for two parts, or the corrected wording, which is claimed proved; (ii) the first-argument date for the IMRN work, where I use the journal date because no earlier public version was verified, while a 2024 preprint is reported and not found; (iii) whether the centered-nonagonal part belongs to this bullet, which I included because the current article lists it.
competing_reading: Read 'Pollock's conjectures' as the 1843/1850 wording. Then the icosahedral and dodecahedral parts were answered negatively (95 and 79), the tetrahedral and octahedral parts remain open, and the corrected 15/22 theorems are a separate question. Under that reading the window contains refutations and a corrected-statement theorem, not a resolution. The opposite reading: the corrected theorems are what the problem became, and Wikipedia's 'confirmed true in 2025' is the status. Both readings depend on whether the IMRN 2025 date counts, and on the computational gap noted above.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The IMRN full text: the exact statements of Theorems 1.7–1.8, whether 95 and 79 appear with a source, Section 9.3 and reference [7]. (2) The discoverer and date of the 95 and 79 counterexamples. (3) The full arXiv PDF of 2608.08019 for acknowledgements and any AI-use statement. (4) Whether a 2024 preprint exists, and its date and contents. (5) Whether the computed ranges in the README cover [9.6446×10³⁵, 10³⁶) and [5.04×10³⁸, 10³⁹), or whether the paper's Section 9.3 does. (6) The January 2024 Wikipedia revision, to see which parts (e)–(g) were listed then. (7) The source of the 4.71×10²⁰ tetrahedral verification claim. (8) The full text of the Nedoshev–Kyrychenko paper, for any stated verification range.
